identity.title: Nystagmus: direction-changing / vertical / pure torsional (central) vs unidirectional horizontal (peripheral)

technique.how: With the patient looking straight ahead, then about 30 degrees right and left (avoid extreme gaze), watch for spontaneous nystagmus and note the fast-phase direction in each position. Peripheral nystagmus is horizontal(-torsional), beats the same direction in all positions and increases when looking toward the fast phase; central patterns are gaze-direction-changing, vertical, or purely torsional.
technique.prerequisites: Spontaneous nystagmus must be present (acute vestibular syndrome); remove fixation if possible (Frenzel lenses or penlight cover test) because fixation suppresses peripheral nystagmus.

interpretation.positive_finding: Nystagmus that reverses direction with gaze (right-beating on right gaze, left-beating on left gaze), vertical (down- or up-beating), or purely torsional nystagmus indicates a central lesion; in the HINTS cohort it was never seen with peripheral AVS.
interpretation.negative_finding: Unidirectional horizontal nystagmus that obeys Alexander law is consistent with vestibular neuritis, but many cerebellar and lateral medullary strokes show exactly this pattern, so it does not exclude stroke on its own (LR about 0.8).
interpretation.pitfalls: End-gaze physiologic nystagmus at extreme lateral gaze is normal; a few beats of symmetric end-point nystagmus is not direction-changing nystagmus. Alcohol, sedatives, and anticonvulsants cause gaze-evoked nystagmus.
interpretation.changes_what: Central-pattern nystagmus: treat as posterior-circulation stroke, MRI and stroke pathway. Peripheral pattern: still requires head impulse and skew testing before accepting a peripheral diagnosis.

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute vestibular syndrome (stroke, hemorrhage, other central lesion)
estimates.population: 101 consecutive AVS patients with >=1 stroke risk factor (25 peripheral, 76 central), examined by neurologists/neuro-ophthalmologist
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (DWI) or CT plus clinical follow-up; peripheral lesions required normal MRI
estimates.computed_from: Table 1 proportions: direction-changing horizontal nystagmus present in 0% of 25 peripheral and 20% of 76 central AVS; sensitivity = 0.20, specificity = 1 - 0.00 = 1.00. NLR 0.80 (0.72-0.90) as reported. LR+ undefined (no false positives). Prevalence 76/101.
estimates.location: Table 1 (Key clinical features in patients with peripheral versus central AVS), PMC4593511

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute vestibular syndrome
estimates.population: Same 101-patient high-risk AVS cohort; finding = dominantly vertical or torsional nystagmus
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (DWI) or CT plus clinical follow-up
estimates.computed_from: Table 1 proportions: dominantly vertical or torsional nystagmus in 0% of 25 peripheral and 12% of 76 central AVS; sensitivity 0.12, specificity 1.00; NLR 0.88 (0.81-0.96) as reported.

sources.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.

Tarnutzer AA, Berkowitz AL, Robinson KA, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. Does my dizzy patient have a stroke? A systematic review of bedside diagnosis in acute vestibular syndrome. CMAJ. 2011;183(9):E571-E592.
Froehling DA, Silverstein MD, Mohr DN, Beatty CW. The rational clinical examination. Does this dizzy patient have a serious form of vertigo? JAMA. 1994;271(5):385-388.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not interpretable when no spontaneous nystagmus is present (episodic or positional vertigo); use Dix-Hallpike or other evaluation instead.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Direction-changing, vertical, or pure torsional nystagmus in acute vertigo is a central sign; do not discharge on a peripheral diagnosis, obtain MRI.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Estimates come from expert neuro-otology examiners; non-expert recognition of nystagmus type is known to be less reliable (see Ohle 2020 HINTS meta-analysis, PMID 32167642).

extraction_notes: Sensitivity/specificity derived from Table 1 group percentages in Kattah 2009 (PMC full text); the table reports only the negative LR, so LR+ is left null (zero false positives). Tarnutzer 2011 CMAJ pooled table not accessible (PMC abstract-only deposit) and Froehling 1994 RCE has no retrievable abstract; both are cited as context without estimates. Two verbatim table rows are given with en-dashes normalized to hyphens.
